Yunqi Monastery.

The *Lin’an Zhi* by Song Xianchun states: "The temple is named Yunqi (Cloud Dwelling). (Appears in the fifteenth leaf of the section on Temples and Observatories. It is located behind Wuyun Mountain in Qiántáng.
A detailed account is provided in the 'Inscription for Yunqi. In the second year of the Zhìpíng era, it was renamed Qīzhēn Temple (Temple of Dwelling in Truth), but today it is known as Yunqi."
"To restore what was old.

[This is from] the "Knowing What Comes First and What Comes Last" chapter of the *Daxue* (Great Learning), a sacred scripture: "Things have their roots and branches; affairs have their beginnings and ends. To know what comes first and what comes last is to draw near to the Way."
[It is] so. Commentary: That which is first at the beginning is what precedes; that which is last at the end is what follows.

To maintain the concise while applying it extensively—Mencius said: "Words that are near yet point to what is remote are excellent words; to maintain the concise while applying it extensively is the excellent Way."
[This is] so. Commentary: "To guard what is concise" refers to cultivating one's person; "to bestow what is broad" refers to bringing peace to the world.
This corresponds to the *Zhongyong* passage: "The Way of the superior man is pervasive yet hidden. Even the ignorance of husband and wife can participate in its knowledge. As for that...
As for its ultimate perfection: even a sage has things he does not know. As for its ordinary practice: even an unworthy husband and wife can perform it.
But as for its ultimate perfection: even a sage has things he cannot achieve.
Seeking the Buddha-wisdom within fundamental wisdom, the *Profound Discourse on the Avataṃsaka* states:
"When truth and falsehood interpenetrate, one perceives the Buddha-mind through the ordinary mind; when principle and phenomena are cultivated together."
One seeks the Buddha-wisdom by means of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Fundamental wisdom is the wisdom inherently possessed by sentient beings;
Buddha-wisdom is the wisdom of the ultimate fruition-Buddha.
Regarding the failure to paint a tiger:
during the reign of Emperor Guangwu of the Eastern Han, General-in-Chief Ma Yuan, while campaigning against the Man people, sent a letter to admonish his son, saying:

"If you do not succeed in emulating Ji Liang, you will fall into being counted among the frivolous and superficial men of the world. This is what is meant by the saying: "Failing to paint a tiger results in something resembling a dog."
Furthermore, "to fall back one *chou*" refers to counting with *chou*.
When Zhang Liang said, "I beg to borrow your former chopsticks to deliberate upon this," it was precisely this. Moreover, in antiquity, when drinking and gambling, they used...
The tally was recorded as a penalty. Yang Zuan was angry that Master Yin had not agreed with his judgment and wished to change it.
He took up his brush and pondered for a long time, then said, "Zuan loses one tally."
When a brother-in-law’s wife was drowning, Mencius rescued her with his hand.

Chun said, "According to the rites, men and women do not touch one another when giving or receiving things. Is this proper? Mencius replied, "It is proper. But when a brother-in-law’s wife is drowning, should one not rescue her with one's hand?
To fail to rescue a drowning brother-in-law’s wife is the act of a wolf or a jackal. That men and women do not touch one another when giving or receiving things is the rule of propriety."
This is the way of ritual propriety (*li*). To rescue one's sister-in-law from drowning by using one's own hands is an exercise of expedient means (*quan*).
As for Wangsun Jia leaning against his gate and watching:
he was a minister of King Min of Qi. When Naochi assassinated King Min, Wangsun Jia had as yet no intention of punishing the rebel.
He returned to visit his mother. His mother said, "If you go out in the morning and return late, I lean against the gate and watch for you.
If you go out in the evening and do not return, I lean against the lintel of the door and watch for you. Now you serve the King, yet the King has fled; you do not know his whereabouts.
With what face can you stand before the world? Thereupon, Jia mobilized the people of the state to attack Naochi.
"The gentleman is ashamed of his words and exceeds in his actions" (from the *Analects*).
In all matters, one must take the ancients as one's teacher.
Fu Yue replied to Gaozong of Shang: "To conduct affairs without taking antiquity as one's teacher, yet to be able to endure for all time—this is something I, Fu Yue, have never heard of.
The *Book of Poetry* states: "The father says, 'I am your support';

the mother says, 'I am your reliance. Without a father, what is there to support? Without a mother, what is there to rely upon? "Support" (*hu*) conveys the sense of providing shelter and protection; "reliance" (*shi*) conveys the sense of depending and trusting.
"The virtue of their toilsome labor is as vast as Heaven and has no limit," says the *Book of Poetry*.
"Alas, alas, my parents! They gave me life through their toilsome labor; the virtue I wish to repay is as vast as Heaven and has no limit."

The *Mingling* (Silkworm Moth) is a different species, as stated in the *Classic of Poetry*: "The *mingling* has offspring; the *guoluo* carries them. Teach and instruct your children, so that they may become good and resemble you.
One cherishes this [lesson] throughout one's entire life.
Mencius said: "When a person is young, he yearns for his parents; when he comes to know and appreciate beauty, he yearns for youthful charms;

when he has a wife and children, he yearns for his wife and children; when he holds office, he yearns for his ruler. When he does not find favor with his ruler, he becomes distressed within. Only the great filial son yearns for his parents throughout his life.
As for one who yearned for them until the age of fifty, I have seen such a person in the Great Shun."

"Moving to the left or right without fixed direction" (*Zuoyou wufang*) appears in the *Tángōng* chapter of the *Lǐjì*. Regarding the service of one's parents: there is concealment [of their faults] but no offense [against them]. Moving to the left or right to attend to their needs is done without fixed direction; in the regular inspections [of their well-being], one never fails [to be present].

From the "Qu Li Shang" (General Rules, Part One) of the *Book of Rites*: "In all cases, one who is a son should keep his father warm in winter and cool in summer; he should settle him at dusk and inquire after him at dawn.
Having exhausted his mental and physical efforts,"
Mencius said, "The way of Yao and Shun could not bring peace and order to the world without benevolent government.
He further said, "Having exhausted one's mental and physical efforts, if this is followed by a government that cannot bear [the suffering of] others, then benevolence will cover the whole world."
"The function of the mind is to think; the function of the mind is to think.
If one thinks, one attains [the truth]; if one does not think, one does not attain it" (from the *Mencius*. "Function" (*guān*) means an office or official;
it refers to a specific charge or duty. "Attain" (*dé*) means to grasp its underlying principle).
"When sincerity reaches its ultimate limit, one communicates with the ghosts and spirits.
As the *Guanzi* says: "Think of it, think of it; think of it again and yet again. If you cannot grasp it through thinking, the ghosts and spirits will surely communicate it to you.
It is not that the ghosts and spirits communicate it, but rather that the limit of one's sincerity has been reached."

When the Son of Heaven was a mere youth, Emperor Gao of Han first rose in rebellion. Wei无知 (Wu Zhi) recommended Chen Ping, saying his talent was fit for use, and appointed him as Commandant of the Central Army.
Upon the acquisition of the empire, when meritorious officials were enfeoffed, Chen Ping was granted the title of Marquis of Quyu. Chen Ping said, "I am not [the equal of] Wei Wu..."
[Chen Ping] said, "I know. By what means could I have advanced? I wish to yield my fief. The Emperor said, "Chen Ping may indeed be called one who does not turn his back on his roots.

He then appointed Wei Wuzhi to office. When Chen Ping was in his humble days, he was dividing meat for the village altar; it was very even. The elder of the altar praised the youth for being a skilled butcher.
Chen Ping said, "If I were to govern the world, I would do so as I did with this meat. The elder then knew him by this.
Name. To use a shell to measure the ocean or rely on a tube to peer at the heavens.
Dongfang Shuo’s "Answering the Guest’s Difficulty" says: "To peer at the heavens through a tube, to measure the ocean with a shell, and to strike a bell with a staff—how [could these suffice]?"
One can thus penetrate its systematic structure, examine its depths, and bring forth its true resonance.
As the *Fengshui Lianzong Baodian* states:
"Studying the Way through other gates is like an ant attempting to climb a high mountain; reciting the Buddha’s name for rebirth [is like crossing it by boat]."
It is like a sail catching the wind on a following current.
Regarding the field frog and the well minnow, the *Zhuangzi* states:
"The field frog cannot be discoursed with about the sea because it is confined to its marsh. This corresponds to the ninth line of the *Jing* hexagram in the *Yijing*.
The second line: "In the well-valley, an arrow shoots at a minnow;
its gills are exposed.

The *Huayan xuantan* (Profound Discourse on the Avatamsaka) states: "Śrāvakas of superior virtue shut out their sight and hearing from the sublime assembly; Bodhisattvas who have accumulated practices expose [their gills]..."
Regarding "gills and scales at the Dragon Gate": it is said that Bodhisattvas who have merely accumulated practices cannot enter the Great Way of the *Avataṃsaka*.
This is like the three tiers of the Yu Gate; those fish that leap over them but do not pass through must return with their gills exposed.
In the *Song of Realizing the Way*, Yongjia likens it to the light of a firefly, saying: "Two bhikṣus committed acts of lust and killing; Upāli’s firefly-light only increased their karmic bonds.
The Great Being Vimalakīrti instantly dispelled their doubts, just as the blazing sun melts frost and snow."

Śāriputra taught two disciples the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and the meditation on counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*). After practicing for a long time without benefit, their minds desired to turn back from the Path.
They went to see the Buddha. The Buddha asked them what their former worldly occupations had been. The one who practiced counting the breath replied, "I guarded a tomb."

At the burial mound, those practicing the contemplation of impurity were told to practice it by treating it as if they were refining gold vessels. The Buddha instructed two men to exchange their objects of meditation and practice accordingly.
Before long, both attained the fruits of the Path, and their three minds were fully developed.
The *Contemplation Sūtra*, in the chapter on "Birth in the Highest Grade of the Highest Class," states: "First is the mind of utmost sincerity; second is the profound mind;
third is the mind of dedication and the making of vows.
Qian is called Great Birth (*dàshēng*), and Kun is called Vast Birth (*guǎngshēng*).
The Appended Statements say: "As for Qian, when it is still, it is focused; when it moves, it is direct. Thus, the Great is produced from it.
As for Kun, when it is still, it is closed; when it moves, it is opened. Thus, the Vast is produced from it."
The Precious Mirror that Subdued Demons:
Wang Du of the Sui dynasty obtained a precious mirror while serving as a district magistrate. In the district there was a large tree inhabited by a deity;

whenever a magistrate arrived, they were required to offer sacrifices, otherwise the deity would cause calamities. Du ordered his men to suspend the precious mirror from the tree at night. That very night, there was a great storm and thunder.

He went to look at it in the morning; the tree was shattered to pieces, and a large snake lay dead beneath it. He then encountered an inn where he saw a woman of extraordinary beauty in the household.
The host said, "A few months ago, a traveler brought her here and said that he would come to take her away again."
To this day, the matter remains obscure. Du suspected she was not human; he secretly retrieved the mirror, whereupon the woman was struck with terror and begged for her life, saying, "I am a fox.
I have deluded many people. Now that I am at your mercy, I beg you to hide the mirror, and I shall submit to death."
Du said, "Zangjing, can you not hide yourself? The spirit replied, "Illuminated as I am by a divine object, where could I conceal my form?
I wish only to die after one more drink. Du gave him wine; he became deeply intoxicated and fell asleep. When Du went to look at him, an old fox was found dead upon the bed.
There were many other such miraculous occurrences that cannot be fully described.
Regarding the "sickness of seven years," Mencius said:
"Those who today desire to become true kings are like those who, having suffered from a sickness for seven years, seek three-year-old mugwort for their remedy;
it is like trying to repair a dilapidated ox-cart."
Just as an ox, suffering from pulling a cart, destroys the cart, only for its owner to build another;
so too, a person who loathes the body as suffering seeks to extinguish it quickly, not realizing that although this body perishes, they will receive yet another body.
Regarding the "exalted and distinctive birth-body" (*janmakāya-viśeṣa*), there remains room for debate;
some say that the body of sixty million *nayuta* is indeed the birth-body, which is the body of the Pure Land.
It is superior to that of the defiled land. In the defiled land, the birth-body is sixteen feet tall; in the pure land, the birth-body ought to be as high and large as this.
Master Zhili, through thirteen rounds of questions and answers, distinguished this and determined it to be the *vairocana-kāya* (the body of sublime characteristics). (Cited from the *Miaozongchao*).
The Bodhisattva practices six recollections:

recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Sangha, recollection of the devas, recollection of ethical discipline, and recollection of generosity. Regarding the recollection of the Buddha: he is the compassionate guide.

Regarding the recollection of the Dharma: it is the mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. Regarding the recollection of the Sangha: they are the field of merit for humans and devas. Regarding the recollection of the devas: they possess longevity and peace and happiness.
One who contemplates the precepts purifies body and mind. One who contemplates giving universally relieves the poor.
The ten mental states are as follows:

first, one gives rise to great loving-kindness toward sentient beings and harbors no intent to harm; second, one gives rise to great compassion toward sentient beings and harbors no intent to oppress.
1. A mind that does not weary of the Buddha’s teachings. 2. A mind that delights in protecting the Dharma without sparing body or life. 3.
A mind that gives rise to supreme patience toward all phenomena and is free from attachment. 4. A mind of pure intention that does not crave gain, offerings, or honor. 5.
A mind that seeks the Buddha’s knowledge of all modes and never forgets it at any time. 6. A mind that respects and reveres sentient beings without [weariness].
Eight: A mind free from inferiority; not clinging to worldly discourse, one gives rise to a mind of certainty regarding the factors of enlightenment. Nine:
Planting various roots of goodness with a mind that is undefiled and pure. Ten: Regarding all Buddhas, one gives rise to a mind of recollection, having abandoned all signs.

Regarding the fact that the various devas eat from the same vessel yet experience differences in the quality of their food, the *Jingming jing* (Sutra of the Pure Name) states: "For example, when the various devas eat from a single precious vessel, the color and quality of the food differ according to their respective merit."
The three animals cross the same river, yet their depths differ according to their varying gaits.
As the *Yongjia ji* states: "It is like an elephant, a horse, and a rabbit crossing a river; because their legs are of different lengths, they reach different depths."
The ten gates for tracing back to the one:
first, sounds and speech; second, the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables; third, taking all four factors collectively; fourth, all phenomena manifesting meaning.

Five. The objects of perception are subsumed within mind-only. Six. Harmonizing conditions to enter emptiness. Seven. The non-obstruction between principle and phenomena. Eight. Universally subsuming all that is signified. Nine.
The non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena. Ten. The brilliant manifestation of the ocean-seal samādhi.

Regarding the performance of Buddha-work through fragrant food, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "In the Land of Universal Fragrance, the Tathāgata Saṃghagandha performs Buddha-work by means of fragrant food.
To the Venerable Anabhilāpya, there is neither speaking nor hearing."

Śūnyatā-utpanna was sitting in meditation within a stone chamber. From the sky, Śakra Devendra scattered flowers as an offering. Śūnyatā-utpanna asked, "Who is scattering these flowers? He replied, "I am Śakra, the Lord of Devas.

[Śūnyatā-utpanna asked,] "For what reason are you scattering these flowers? He replied, "Because the Venerable One has skillfully expounded the Prajñāpāramitā. The Venerable One said, "In truth, I have not expounded anything.
Śakra said, "Since the Venerable One has not expounded anything, I likewise have not heard anything. "Neither has there been any hearing," [the Venerable One continued].
To speak of "no-hearing" is truly to speak of Prajñāpāramitā.
The school has ten gates:
first, both self and dharmas exist; second, dharmas exist while the self is non-existent; third, dharmas have no past or future; fourth, the present encompasses both the provisional and the real.
Five. The conventional is false while the ultimate is real. Six. All phenomena are merely names. Seven. The three natures are empty yet existent. Eight.
True emptiness transcends all marks. Nine. Emptiness and existence are unimpeded. Ten. Perfect interfusion and the possession of all virtues.
Regarding the five translators, including Lokakṣema and others:
Lokakṣema was a person of the Later Han period. Because Emperor Guangwu restored the dynasty, it is called the Later Han. Emperor Ming was the son of Guangwu. Kang Sengkai was a person of Wei;
when Cao Pi succeeded the Han, the state name became Wei. Zhi Qian lived during the era of Sun Wu in the Three Kingdoms period.
Ren (人): Fa-xian of the Song dynasty; a person of the Vast Song period. Bo-ti-liu-zhi (菩提流志) of the Northern Wei; a person of the Northern and Southern Dynasties during the Wei.
He was of the Tuoba clan, who changed their surname to Yuan and established the state known as Wei.
During the Zhou dynasty there was the Qin of the Ying clan, and during the Southern and Northern Dynasties there were the Fu Qin and Yao Qin.
In the time of the Zhou, there was one named Feizi, a descendant of Bo Yi, who was skilled at raising horses. King Ping of Zhou favored him and enfeoffed him at Shan;
his state was named Qin, thus becoming the Qin of the Ying clan. "Ying" was his surname. As for the Fu Qin, they were a Di tribe during the Eastern Jin period.
Fu Jian was powerful and strong; he occupied Guanzhong, and his state was also called Qin, known as the Fu Qin. The Yao Qin were of Qiang descent.
Yao Chang had served as a general under Fu Jian; later, when Jian was defeated by the Jin, Chang subsequently took control of Guanzhong and passed the throne to his son, Yao Xing.
This refers to the Yao Qin dynasty.
According to the *Zhou Li*, the officials who managed the languages of the four quarters were designated as follows:
those for the east were called *ji*, for the south *xiang*, for the west *didi*, and for the north *yi*; these were all official titles.
"Ji" (to lodge) signifies that one can lodge within the differences of customs here; "xiang" (to imitate) signifies that one can imitate the differences of customs there.
"Di" (shoes) is intended to distinguish the differences in clothing and adornment; "yi" (translate) is intended to discern the differences in speech.
In the *Zhouguan* (Rites of Zhou), they are collectively termed *xiangxu*; in common parlance, they are generally called *yi*. Furthermore, "yi" means "to explain.
It is synonymous with "to transcribe" (*teng*), meaning that one transcribes and explains the languages of both parties to facilitate communication between them.

In the thirteenth year of the Jianyuan era of Fu Jian of the Qin dynasty, he dispatched the general Lü Guang to invade Kucha; having defeated them, Lü Guang led his troops back to Liangzhou, where he subsequently seized the province and styled himself King of Liang.
After Lü Guang died, his nephew Lü Long surrendered to the Jin dynasty, who then invited Master Shi to enter [the capital].
Guān resided at the Xiāoyáo Garden.
He produced ten commentaries on the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra*,
the *Buddha-śāsana-sūtra*, the *Prajñā-pāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, the *Śrī-guṇavyūha-sūtra*, and the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* for the purpose of their circulation.
The *Sūtra*, the *Acintyavimokṣa-sūtra*, the *Anantamukha-sūtra*, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra*, the *Amitābha-sūtra*, and the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
He was renowned in the world as the commentator on these ten sūtras.
Their multitude is beyond counting.
As the *Shi* says: "The descendants of Shang, their multitude is beyond counting.
(*Bao Wang Lun*)
Dharma Master Feixi of Caotang composed the *Nianfo Sanmei Baowang Lun* (Treatise on the Jewel King of the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection).
Layman Wang Rixiu of Longshu and others composed the *Jingtu Wen* (Texts on the Pure Land). The Layman Wujin Zhang Shangying had a request [to compose such works].
The *Text on Rebirth in the Pure Land* was written by Wang Gu-zhi, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
The *Collection for Resolving Doubts about the Pure Land* was composed by the Śramaṇa Da-you of Wu-jun. The *Record of Self-Confidence in the Pure Land* was written by the Layman Wu-gong, Wang Tian.
The *Brief Biography of the Pure Land Repentance Master* was composed by Zun-shi, the Master of Repentance at Ci-yun Monastery.

The Verses of Master Shandao on the Practice of the Direct Path: "Gradually the skin becomes like chicken-skin and the hair like crane-feathers; look at the gait, growing increasingly tottering. (And so forth...
Only the practice of the direct path remains: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha."
The Chan Master Yongming Shou composed the "Fu on the Spirit Dwelling in An-yang" (Shenqi Anyang Fu),
as well as various poems on longing for the Pure Land.
Master Zhongfeng Ben of the Song dynasty, Master Xizhai Chushi Qi of the Yuan dynasty, and others— The branches bend low only because they support the golden terrace;
My Master ascended the first stage in a single thought, And twice has come to the Buddhist realm amidst the music of flutes and songs. Only at the gate before me... (etc.)
Konggu Long Chan Master (皇明空谷隆禪師) of the Ming Dynasty, of the Konggu and Dufeng lineages, has the *Konggu ji* (Collected Works of Konggu). Chan Master Dufeng Shan has a *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings).
Chan Master Tianqi Rui, whose sobriquet was Qiongjue Lao Ren (Old Man of Solitude), has the *Qiongjue ji* (Collected Works of Solitude).
All the stars revolve toward the North Star.
As the *Analects* says: "To govern by means of virtue is like the North Star (Beichen), which remains in its place while all the stars revolve around it."
Yuanzhao (originally named Lianjing) of the Song dynasty was from Wuxi, Changzhou.
Initially, he studied under Chan Master Tiandi Huai; through the practice of *nianfo*, he attained awakening. Later, he moved to Jingci Monastery.

There, Dharma Master Leifeng Cai traveled in spirit to the Pure Land and beheld a flower of extraordinary beauty. When asked about it, [the master] said: [The text continues with the description of the flower and its significance.]
He waited for Chan Master Ben of Jingci and Master Xi of Zifu; when they arrived at Huilin, he prostrated at their feet, offered gold, and departed.
When people questioned him about his reason, he said, "In my meditative concentration, I saw golden lotus flowers. People told me to wait for the Chan Master.
Thus, although the Master belonged to the Chan school, he concurrently cultivated the Pure Land. Later, he passed away while sitting upright; he was posthumously titled Yuanzhao.
Sengrui, the Lotus Emerging from the Couch:
Sengrui followed Dharma Master Kumārajīva to receive the teachings on the meaning of the sutras. Later, he joined the Lotus Society at Mount Lu.

In the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying, "I am about to depart. Facing west with palms joined, he passed away. The assembly beheld Sengrui...
A single golden lotus before his couch suddenly vanished, and five-colored fragrant smoke issued forth from his chamber.
Wen Lu-gong (Wen Poxuan) and Su Chang-gong (Su Shi Yanbo) served as Prime Ministers of the Song dynasty;
Wen was titled Duke of Lu, while Su Shi served as Hanlin Academician. Su Shi’s younger brother was Su Zhe.
Both possessed great reputations; thus, he was styled Changgong (the Elder).
Qibo of Qi and Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor, engaged in a dialogue that produced works such as the *Neijing* (Inner Canon), making him the patriarch of the medical tradition.
Qingzhao recited a verse as he returned to the West.

Huìhéng resided at Wǔ'ān and was known as the Vinaya Master Qingzhao Yǎnshòu. Initially, he relied on Língzhī Temple to study the Vinaya, and for sixty years he specialized in the practice of Pure Land Buddhism.
At the time of his death, he gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha’s name and spoke this verse for them: "Maitreya, Maitreya."

Recite [the name] while contemplating the white curl between the eyebrows at every thought-moment. Holding this non-retrogressive mind, one will certainly be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).
Ge Jizhi of Jurong, during the Song dynasty, abandoned his studies of the immortals and turned his heart toward pure karma.
His wife, Lady Ji, alone maintained singular sincerity in the recitation of the Buddha’s name. At the beginning...
In the third year of the Jià era, while she was at her loom, she suddenly perceived a clarity in the air.
She stopped her weaving and looked up toward the four quarters of the sky, where she saw the Buddha manifesting in the west, with precious canopies, banners, and streamers outshining the Milky Way.

Overjoyed, she said, "The Sūtras speak of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; could this be him? She prostrated herself before the Buddha. Jì was struck with wonder and approached her; Jǐ氏 pointed [to the vision].

He was shown the Buddha’s dwelling place; while being ferried across, he also saw half of the Buddha’s body, which suddenly vanished. Five-colored auspicious clouds appeared, witnessed by all his kinsmen.
From that time on, they all returned to the Buddha-dharma.

Tánluán of the Later Wèi dynasty burned the *Xiānjīng* (Scripture on the Immortals) and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of the *Guānjīng* (Scripture on Contemplation). By nature, he was fond of the pursuit of longevity. He had received ten fascicles of the *Xiānjīng* from Táo Yǐnjūn.
Later, upon meeting Bódhíliúzhī, he asked: "Does the Buddha possess a technique for longevity and immortality? Bódhíliúzhī smiled and said: "Longevity and immortality..."

"This is my Buddha-way. He then bestowed upon him the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations*. "If you study this, you shall no longer be born within the three realms, nor shall you again wander through the six paths of existence.
As for its longevity, even the sands of the Ganges or kalpa-stones cannot compare to it.
This is the 'long life' of our Golden Immortal (the Buddha). Tandi was greatly delighted; he subsequently burned his Daoist scriptures and cultivated the practices of purity.
After Chan Master Yongming Shou passed away, a monk came from Lin’an and circumambulated the master’s stupa for a year. When people asked him the reason, he said:
"I was ill and entered the underworld. There I saw the image of a monk enshrined to the left of the hall, to whom the King paid diligent homage and respect. He spoke this in secret.
When he inquired about this person, they said: "This is Chan Master Yongming Shou of Hangzhou.

All who die must pass through the underworld, yet this master has already been born directly into the Western Paradise in the highest grade. Because of his virtue, the King pays him respectful homage."
There was a rākṣasa named Xiuxin who lived in a certain village. The people of that village used to send their children daily as food for him.
However, there was one son who had taken refuge in the Triple Gem and single-mindedly recited the Buddha’s name; consequently, he could not be eaten and was able to return home.
The *Yi* says:
"Deliberate before you speak; deliberate before you act. Through deliberation, one perfects their transformations.
Divination is used to resolve doubt; if there is no doubt, what need is there for divination?
When Emperor Taizong of the Tang was still the Prince of Qin, he harbored mutual resentment toward Crown Prince Jiancheng and intended to raise an army.

When his subordinates deliberated on the matter, they feared they would not prevail, so he ordered a divination to be performed. Zhang Gongjin took the tortoise shell and threw it to the ground, saying, "Divination is for resolving doubts; if there is no doubt, why divinate?"
△ Second Fascicle:
